text: Every continent on Earth is moving. And one day, they'll all crash back together.
It's happened before. About three hundred million years ago, almost all land was one supercontinent: Pangaea.
That's why fossils of the same little reptile turn up in both Brazil and South Africa.
So what if all the continents reunited?
You could drive from New York to London. No planes, no ferries.
Today, ships carry about eighty percent of world trade. Trucks and trains would take over.
But the middle of the continent would be brutal, farther from the sea than anywhere on Earth today.
With no ocean to calm the weather, summers could top forty degrees, and winters could freeze hard.
Rain clouds would dry out long before they reached the centre, leaving giant deserts.
Pangaea had them. Its sand dunes turned to stone, and became the red cliffs of Zion National Park.
The coasts, though, would get megamonsoons: rainy seasons even wilder than India's.
And there'd be just one giant ocean. Fewer coastlines means less shallow sea, where much of ocean life lives.
Where continents collide, the land crumples up into mountains.
Pangaea's central mountains may have rivalled the Himalayas. Today, they're the worn-down Appalachians.
But don't panic. This can't happen suddenly. Continents move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
So the next supercontinent is about two hundred and fifty million years away.
And one study found it could be so hot that mammals could survive on only about a tenth of it.
Here's the twist: Earth has done this at least three times. Pangaea was just the latest.
One planet. One continent. One ocean. And we're already on our way there.
